fatal_errors: The proposed Cu-cap intervention does not reconstruct the studied interventions of 700 K annealing, elastic tensile strain, or ribbon-spacing control.
It attributes magnetic hysteresis and entropy-change behavior to dynamic thermal gradients without evidence that such gradients govern the reported quasi-static magnetometry.
A 5 nm Cu cap is assumed to improve heat extraction, but no heat-flow geometry or thermal model shows that it would materially alter conductance relative to the substrate interface.
The initial material is incorrectly described as grain-boundary-rich; the target films were amorphous or extremely fine/disordered with no detectable long-range crystalline order.
The cited evidence does not establish Cu-capping effects, thermal-gradient-controlled magnetocaloric behavior, or the proposed mechanism in Fe25Ni21Mn24Si13Ge17 films or ribbons.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad thin-film magnetocaloric and hysteresis problem and offers a reasonably clear three-arm experiment with an explicit falsification rule. However, it is a speculative alternative rather than a reconstruction of the target study. The target response was governed primarily by short-range atomic reordering and internal-strain relaxation after 700 K annealing, magnetoelastic effects under 0–2% strain, and spacing-dependent inter-ribbon coupling. Its magnetocaloric entropy change was measured from isotherms up to 50 kOe, not under the proposed sub-100 mT cycling conditions. Generic literature on stress-mediated domain pinning supports only a peripheral part of the mechanism; none of the cited evidence validates thermal bottlenecks or Cu capping as the controlling factor. Although measuring thermal resistance alongside magnetic response is discriminating, matched caps and rate-dependent measurements would also be required to separate thermal transport from Cu-induced strain, interdiffusion, oxidation protection, or magnetic-interface effects.
